findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: The PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common. Any third-party or downstream CryptoProvider implementation compiled against a previous keycloak-common version does not implement this method. With the new `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` code, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` invokes `order()` on every provider found by the ServiceLoader, so an older compiled provider will throw `AbstractMethodError` during `CryptoIntegration.init`, completely failing startup instead of just being sorted differently. Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve binary/source compatibility for existing implementations.

findings.title: Multiple real providers with equal order() are now silently resolved by classpath order instead of failing fast
findings.body: Previously, `detectProvider` threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which caught misconfigured deployments. Now providers are sorted by `order()` descending and the first is silently used, with the rest only logged at debug level. However all three 'real' providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return the same order value 200, so if two of their jars end up on the classpath together, the winner is decided by ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order — non-obvious and environment-dependent. This is especially risky for FIPS: if both crypto/default and crypto/fips1402 jars are present, the non-FIPS provider may silently be selected (and even when FIPS wins, merely instantiating DefaultCryptoProvider during ServiceLoader iteration registers the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider in the JVM security provider list as a constructor side effect). Equal-order ties among full providers should still be treated as a configuration error rather than silently picked.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns whatever JCA provider backs the default keystore (typically the SUN provider) — not a BouncyCastle provider as the interface contract (`@return BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider`) documents. Any caller that obtains this provider and then requests BouncyCastle-specific algorithms or keystores (e.g. BCFKS, PKCS7Padding via BC) from it will fail at runtime, and callers that use a non-null return value as a signal that BouncyCastle is available will be misled. WildFlyElytronProvider demonstrates that returning null is an accepted implementation; if the authz-client genuinely has no BouncyCastle, this should return null (or the contract/hack should be documented) rather than returning an unrelated provider.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion test only round-trips through the same implementation, so it cannot catch standard-noncompliant DER encoding
findings.body: The new test verifies `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` by feeding the output of `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` back into `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` and asserting equality. Because both directions are implemented by the same new ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder code, any self-consistent but incorrect encoding still passes — for example, if both the encoder and decoder used a wrong tag constant for INTEGER or SEQUENCE, or mis-encoded lengths, the round-trip assertion would still succeed while real Keycloak servers would reject the produced JWS signatures. The primary purpose of this PR is producing standard DER signatures for ES256/ES384/ES512 client authentication without BouncyCastle, so the test should additionally verify the DER output against an independent implementation (e.g. `Signature.verify` with the JCA Signature, or fixed known-answer test vectors comparing against BouncyCastle's encoding), and ideally cover the end-to-end AuthzClient-with-ES256-credentials path.
